title: AMAT and measured cost
description: Hit time, miss penalty and the stall in *timed mode*: predict AMAT, then compare it with what was measured.

steps.text: Timed mode charges fixed costs: a hit takes 1 cycle, and a miss takes that 1 cycle plus a miss penalty of 20 cycles, during which the CPU stalls waiting for memory. The *average memory access time*, AMAT, is the hit time plus the miss rate times the miss penalty. The trace has ten accesses.
Four of the ten accesses will miss, so the miss rate is 0.40. What is the AMAT?
steps.hint: AMAT = hit time + miss rate × miss penalty. The hit time is 1 and the penalty is 20.
Press Run in the transport bar. If the trace has already run, press Reset, then Run.

steps.text: Find a Stall in the log: drag the timeline to it and look at the CPU. While memory answers a miss, the CPU waits.
The Stats show AMAT of 9.0 cycles, but the measured cost is higher: 110 cycles over 10 accesses. Why does the measurement differ from AMAT?
options: AMAT leaves out the write-back of the dirty line
steps.explain: The last miss evicted a dirty line, and writing it back costs another miss penalty. AMAT counts only the misses, not the write-backs they cause.
steps.hint: The first access was a store. What happens to its line when `0x080` takes its place?

steps.text: Cycles: 10 accesses at 1, plus 4 misses at 20, plus 1 write-back at 20, is 110, or 11.0 per access. AMAT gives 9.0; the write-back adds 20 over 10 accesses, which is the extra 2.0 in the Measured line. AMAT is the rule of thumb, and a write-back is a cost it does not see.
